# Pañcāvudhajātaka (Ja 55)

**ID:** Ja 55
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Pañcāvudhajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Five Weapons
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja55
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Pañcāvudhajātaka* (Ja 55) is a birth story of the Pali *Jātaka* collection [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. Its framing story (*paccuppannavatthu*) is set at Jetavana, delivered by the Buddha concerning a monk who had abandoned all energetic effort (*ossatthaviriyo*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. The opening verse begins with the words *Yo alīnena cittenā* ("When no attachment / with undaunted mind") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877].

In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as Prince Pañcāvudha ("Five Weapons"), the son of King Brahmadatta of Bārāṇasī [Fausböll 1877; Lamotte 1970]. When he reaches sixteen years of age—the age of discretion—he completes his training in arts and archery in Takṣaśilā in Gandhāra, where his teacher gives him a set of five weapons (bow and arrows, sword, spear, club, and shield) [Horner 1930; Lamotte 1970]. Returning home through a wilderness forest, he encounters the terrifying, violent yakṣa Silesaloma ("Sticky Hair"), who attacks travelers [Appleton 2014; Lamotte 1970]. Prince Pañcāvudha attacks the demon by shooting arrows and hurling his weapons, but all stick harmlessly in the ogre's hair; he then strikes with his right and left hands, right and left feet, and his head, so that his five limbs are also trapped against the monster's body [Lamotte 1970]. Despite being completely caught, the prince remains fearless and undaunted, demonstrating bodily and mental non-withdrawal (*vīrya*) [Sahni 2008; Lamotte 1970]. Moved by his fearlessness and taught the moral and karmic consequences of violence, the demon releases him, accepts conversion, and undertakes the five precepts [Sahni 2008; Lamotte 1970]. In the *samodhāna*, the yakṣa is identified as a former birth of the converted murderer Aṅgulimāla, while Prince Pañcāvudha was the Buddha himself; hearing the teaching, the discouraged monk attains arahantship [Appleton 2014; Fausböll 1877].

Parallel narrative versions celebrating heroic exertion appear widely in northern and Chinese Buddhist literature, notably in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra*, the *Za baozang jing* (T 203), and the *Jiu za piyu jing*, where the protagonist is called Simha ("Lion") [Lamotte 1970]. DharmaNexus matches show internal Pali text reuse in the nidāna segment (§0.1–2.1) shared with the following *Kañcanakkhandhajātaka* (Ja 56) [DharmaNexus]. In modern times, the motif of fearlessness and self-abnegation in the *Pañcāvudhajātaka* was invoked within modernizing Theravāda discourse and during the Burmese independence movement [Sarkisyanz 1965].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Kañcanakkhandhajātaka (Ja 56) (§0.1–2.1 ↔ §0.1–2.1)

- [Fausböll 1877] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka Together with Its Commentary, Vol. 1 (1877) — Pali text incipit, occasion at Jetavana regarding an ossatthaviriya monk, and concluding samodhāna.
